The Times analysis of service bulletins was limited to General Motors. The safety agency declined to comment on how G.M. compared with other automakers, but its top defects investigator, Frank Borris, last year scolded G.M. over its lack of responsiveness on safety issues, in contrast to its peers.
“The general perception is that G.M. is slow to communicate, slow to act, and, at times, requires additional effort,” Mr. Borris wrote to Carmen Benavides, director of product investigations at G.M., in a July 2013 email. The company, he added, required effort from the agency “that we do not feel is necessary with some of your peers.”
In one case, he reprimanded G.M. for issuing a service bulletin in July 2012 for a “fairly obvious” safety concern over a defective air bag in the Buick Verano and Chevrolet Cruze and Sonic. G.M. recalled some of the cars in October 2012, expanded the recall in January 2013 and eventually recalled even more in November.
Mr. Borris also cited four other instances in which the agency questioned G.M.’s use of technical bulletins to deal with safety issues and pressed for recalls, including the case of the 2013 Chevrolet Malibu, which was recalled in May 2012 for an air bag defect.
The automaker’s top product executive, Mark Reuss, declined to say whether G.M. had a pattern of issuing service bulletins for safety problems before eventually ordering recalls.
“I don’t have any data on that,” he said last week when asked by The Times at an industry event in New York. “We are definitely working on being responsive.”
He added that the company works closely with the safety agency, “but there’s always some tension there.”
Greg Martin, a G.M. spokesman, said in a written statement, “We issue technical service bulletins to our dealers to help ensure specific product issues are diagnosed and repaired properly.”
A spokeswoman for Ford Motor, the second largest American automaker after G.M., also said that the bulletins “are used to help dealers diagnose and repair customers’ vehicles.” The spokeswoman, Kelli Felker, added: “A safety recall addresses production vehicle or component conditions that may present an unreasonable risk to safety.”
Ms. Barra has repeatedly asserted that safety is a core value for the company. At a Senate hearing this month, when asked if the failure to fix the ignition switch in the Cobalts was a one-time event, she said, “I see it as a very extraordinary situation,” then adding, “There have been many, many cases where we’ve been quick to act from a safety recall process.”
Series of Service Bulletins
The review by The Times found multiple instances in which the company used service bulletins instead of immediately recalling cars, with the gap between a bulletin and a recall ranging from six months to nine years.
In the case of the Saturn Ion, which had a power steering system that could suddenly turn off, there were at least three service bulletins issued over a period of nine years before G.M. finally issued a recall last month.
Just last August, Sharon Luers said, she was driving to a friend’s house in Shrewsbury, Pa., in her 2004 Ion when she heard a chime and saw a warning light flash for the power steering. Almost immediately, she lost control of her car. “It took all my strength to pull over,” she said.

A few days later, it happened again.
Beginning in 2005, General Motors issued service bulletins alerting technicians at dealerships that “some customers may comment that the steering wheel is hard to turn and that a message of ‘PWR STR’ is displayed,” as one 2009 bulletin read.
In March 2010, G.M. recalled nearly 1.1 million Cobalts and Pontiac G5s for faulty power steering systems, but the Ion was not recalled, even though it used the same steering system.

By September 2011, G.M. had informed the auto safety agency — which had begun to investigate problems with the Ion — of 3,489 customer reports claiming a sudden loss of power steering in 2004-7 Ions, as well as two crash claims indicating that drivers had been injured, according to regulatory filings. It is not known if any deaths resulted from the problem.
The following month, Ms. Barra, who was then vice president for global product development, received an email from a senior G.M. engineer, telling her that the Ion might have the same power steering problems that led to the recall of the Cobalt and G5.
“Mary,” the email said, “during the initial Cobalt case, the Ion data did not justify being included. The situation has been evolving. We will meet and understand the latest data.”
In May 2012, the company sent out two more bulletins, one for dealers and one for owners. In bold, the letter to owners stated, “Do not take your vehicle to your G.M. dealer as a result of this letter unless you believe that your vehicle has the condition as described above.” Ms. Luers, too, received this letter, but it was not until later that her car showed these symptoms.
Almost two years later, on March 28, G.M. recalled all 2004-7 Ions for the power steering problems, along with six other models.
By that time, more than 1,200 complaints about steering — 42 percent of all complaints about the car — had been filed with regulators. Additionally, a number of Ion owners had taken to online chat forums to discuss the cars, with some expressing confusion about the service bulletins. In 2010, one Ion owner on SaturnFan.com wrote, “Finally there is something, though not a recall.”
Thousands of Complaints
N.H.T.S.A., which closed its investigation into the Ion last Tuesday, cited almost 4,800 complaints about the power steering problem that had been filed with both the safety agency and G.M., as well as more than 30,000 warranty claims at G.M. The regulator also pointed to 12 crashes with evidence linking the incidents to the defect.
The Ion is not the only car that G.M. did not promptly recall when a safety issue became apparent.
In August 2013, G.M. recalled some models of the Chevrolet Cruze because of a defect that could result in a loss of braking assistance. The company had issued a related technical service bulletin in June 2011.
And in May 2013, G.M. recalled certain models of the Buick LaCrosse, Buick Regal and Chevrolet Malibu Eco because of a condition that could lead to stalling and trunk fires. The automaker had issued related technical service bulletins as early as October 2012, for unsold vehicles only, which raised suspicions among regulators, according to Mr. Borris’s email to G.M.
The most glaring example is the defective ignition in the Cobalt, Saturn Ion and other small cars. As far back as 2001, the automaker had known that if the switch was jostled, it could turn off, shutting off the engine and disabling the air bags. In 2005, instead of recalling the cars, G.M. sent dealers a service bulletin suggesting that they tell drivers to remove objects attached to ignition keys. Only this year did the company order a recall of the cars.
Although it is G.M.’s responsibility to report safety problems, Ms. Claybrook, the former N.H.T.S.A. official, said the agency was somewhat culpable for not detecting abuses in service bulletins.
“Part of the problem is that N.H.T.S.A. is so grossly underfunded that it doesn’t have time to read them as they come in,” she said.
The safety agency said that it looks at every technical service bulletin it receives and may open an investigation when appropriate. The Times analysis found that car companies issue thousands of the notices each year and that safety-related bulletins may be lumped in among notices for less serious issues.
Still, automakers are required to act on serious safety problems with a recall. And when they do, it hurts them financially, and more important, in their reputation, said Daniel G. Hill, a crisis expert at Ervin Hill Strategy, a communications firm in Washington, who is familiar with the technical notices.
“But you hope that calculus hasn’t been factored into the decision-making process,” he said.

Robert A. Roe, who as a congressman from New Jersey for 23 years played a key role in financing projects to expand the nation’s highway and mass transit systems and to combat water and ground pollution, died on Tuesday at his home in Green Pond, N.J. He was 90.
His family confirmed the death.
Mr. Roe, a Democrat, was his state’s commissioner of conservation and economic development when he won a special election to the House of Representatives in 1969 to complete the term of Charles S. Joelson, who had resigned.
Mr. Roe was handily re-elected 11 times in his predominantly Democratic district, consisting largely of Passaic County, until he announced in 1992 that he would not run again.
As the head of House subcommittees on economic development and water resources, and later as chairman of the Public Works and Transportation Committee, Mr. Roe helped shape major infrastructure bills. One was the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act of 1991, which authorized $150 billion (about $260 billion in today’s dollars) for rail and other mass transit projects as well as roads.
The act gave states flexibility in how they used the money, reflecting a federal shift in focus from highway projects to other modes of moving people. Mr. Roe, who had championed highway building and who had once dismissed its critics as “people who have made a career out of being environmentalists,” expressed pride in the legislation, telling reporters that “intermodality” was now his favorite word.
He had long supported legislation welcomed by many environmentalists. He helped steer House passage of a bill expanding the
Superfund
program for cleaning land contaminated with toxic wastes. And he was a chief author of a bill, passed in 1987 over President Ronald Reagan’s veto, that provided nearly $20 billion to help municipalities build sewage treatment plants and curb water pollution.
Mr. Reagan called the legislation a “budget buster,” but Mr. Roe, on the House floor, countered: “Clean water is life itself. There is nothing we can do that is a higher priority.”
He also led in advancing bills authorizing harbor, dam, flood-control and erosion-control projects.
Mr. Roe was a favorite of labor unions: More public works projects meant more jobs, a theme he sounded regularly. During President Jimmy Carter’s administration, Vice President Walter F. Mondale referred to him as “Mr. Jobs.”
Like other congressional leaders on public works, Mr. Roe made sure that his district and state benefited. Besides financing for new public buildings and facilities to curb water pollution, he helped bring about new rail links to New Jersey to ease commuting into Manhattan. A federal office building in Paterson is named for Mr. Roe.
He was also diligent in including in legislation projects important to House colleagues from across the country.
His critics accused him of pork-barrel legislating; his defenders said he was simply following an expedient congressional tradition of building bipartisan coalitions to advance public works. Mr. Roe said such home-state projects were a small fraction of the bills.

Mr. Roe rose to chairman of the Science, Space and Technology Committee in the House. As a committee member he had headed its hearing on the explosion of the
space shuttle
Challenger, in which the seven crew members died shortly after liftoff in 1986.
Mr. Roe ran for the Democratic nomination for governor in New Jersey in 1977 and 1981, finishing second each time.
After leaving Congress in January 1993, he became a consultant and lobbyist. That May a car he was driving crashed into a van, seriously injuring its occupants. Mr. Roe, who was not hurt, pleaded guilty to drunken and reckless driving and was sentenced to three years’ probation.
In 2008, when the state named a highway, Route 23, for him, the family of the crash victims and the group Mothers Against Drunk Driving protested. He then declined the honor.
Robert A. Roe was born in Wayne Township, N.J., on Feb. 28, 1924. He served in the Army during World War II, attended Oregon State University and Washington State University, and became a construction company executive. He served as Wayne Township’s mayor and as a Passaic County freeholder before being named the state’s conservation and economic development chief in 1963.
Mr. Roe, who never married and did not have children, is survived by nieces and nephews.

Q. I am used to seeing the top of the
Con Edison clock tower
, off Union Square, lighted up. On April 1, the lights went out and stayed out for quite a while. Was that an April Fools’ joke?
A. Not at all. The purpose was to protect migratory birds in flight.
From midnight until dawn, April 1 to June 1, and again from Sept. 1 through Nov. 1, Con Edison turns off the lights at its 28-story clock tower, at East 14th Street and Irving Place, to help decrease the deaths of migrating birds, who collide with buildings because of the high amount of disorienting artificial light, Robert McGee, a spokesman for Con Edison, said by email.
Scientists are not sure why birds that migrate at night seem to have trouble avoiding bright light sources. “Birds use the stars and moon to navigate, so the extensive light can confuse their natural navigation instincts, often with deadly consequences,” Mr. McGee wrote. “It is estimated that some 90,000 birds die annually in New York City because of collisions with buildings.
“Anyone who lives in a high-rise building can help by turning off lights or pulling down shades in their apartments during the late-night hours. A welcome byproduct of all this is that it saves energy,” Mr. McGee added.
The
Chrysler Building
, Rockefeller Center, Barclays Center and The New York Times Building are among the more than 50 other participants that turn off or dim their exterior lights at night during the migration periods.
Q. Was bingo invented in New York?
A. No, but the name was. The game itself has been traced from an Italian lottery in 1530, Lo Giuoco del Lotto D’Italia, that was introduced in France in the late 1770s, where it was called Le Lotto, according to
About.com
. Germans also played a variation in the 1800s.
In the United States, where it is believed to have first surfaced in 1929 in a carnival near Atlanta, it was called “beano,” after the beans players used to cover their cards. (It is still called Beano in Massachusetts.)
Enter Edwin S. Lowe, a 19-year-old toy maker from Brooklyn, who was at the Atlanta carnival. He asked a few friends back home to play the game, and one of them got so excited at winning, she yelled, “Bingo!” He printed up cards, increased the possible combinations and sold the game as Bingo. His E. S. Lowe Company manufactured Bingo and Yahtzee games, as well as miniature toys and chess and checker sets used by American soldiers during World War II. Milton Bradley bought his company in 1973.
An entrepreneur par excellence, Mr. Lowe branched out into real estate development and Broadway producing. In 1967, he lived in the same luxury cooperative on Fifth Avenue as Gov. Nelson A. Rockefeller, who asked Mr. Lowe for advice on how to liven up the state’s badly slumping lottery. He said he told the governor to “stop pussyfooting around” with advertising that stressed aid to education and to instead focus on ticket buyers’ primary concern: “their hope to hit it rich, and quick.” He said he personally did not play the lottery, “because I’m quite comfortable, and frankly not interested in a get-rich-quick scheme.”
Mr. Lowe died in Manhattan in 1986.

Hiding Purchases
On iTunes
Q.
The Purchased link on the iTunes Store screen lists everything I’ve bought there, including some items I’d rather not have shown on a shared computer. Is there a way to remove selected titles from the list?
A.
Apple allows you to
“hide”
music, books, videos, apps and other content you previously purchased from the company’s various online stores. To remove these items from view, you need to log into your Apple account through the iTunes program on your Windows PC or Mac. If you are not already logged in, open iTunes, go to the Store menu and choose Sign In.
Once you have logged into your account, click the iTunes Store button. On the right side of the main iTunes Store screen, click the Purchased link. This takes you to the list of purchases you have made in that content category (like Movies or Music).
To hide a purchase from view, move the cursor over the item’s thumbnail image. A small black “x” appears in the upper-left corner of the thumbnail. Click the “x” and then click the “Hide” button when the alert box asks you to confirm your decision. Click the content labels (like Music or TV Shows) on the top-right side of the Purchased screen to get to the thumbnails for those items.
If you ever want to see those past purchases, open iTunes and choose View Account from the Store menu. After you log into your account page, scroll down to the “iTunes in the Cloud” section to Hidden Purchases and click the Manage button. Choose the content type you want to reveal and click the Unhide button under the item’s icon to return it to your Purchased list.

TIP OF THE WEEK
The holiday cooking season is here, and if you happen to use a Windows 8.1 laptop or tablet, the
MSN Food & Drink
app serves as a recipe database, meal planner, shopping-list generator and cooking tutor. The app is free from the online
Windows Store
if it is not already installed on your system.
For those who like to cook with the computer in the kitchen, the app features hundreds of recipes in easy-to-read type arranged on step-by-step screens that can be advanced by tapping arrow keys in the screen or keyboard. If you would rather keep sticky fingers off the hardware, though, MSN Food & Drink also includes a hands-free mode that turns the device’s webcam into a basic motion sensor.
To
use the Hands-Free feature
, open a recipe from the Food & Drink app and select the Hands-Free Mode icon at the bottom of the screen. When you have completed the steps on the first recipe screen, move to the next screen by waving your hand in front of the webcam; you can go back a step by waving your hand in the other direction.
